clue.text: One lot appears backward about rent in N Africa

indicators.note: about says the reversed run goes around the word for rent
appearing backward tells us to read the run made by one and lot from right to left

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I
taken as written
a rent is a tear, a rip

explanation.surface: Someone notes a strange reversal in a rent dispute somewhere in North Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: 'appears backward' turns the whole first run, giving TOLI, which 'about' then splits open; 'rent' is a tear, not a payment.
explanation.definitionFit: Tripoli is the capital city of Libya, on the North African coast.

clue.text: House parties arranged in Stroud

indicators.note: arranged says the letters of the town name are put in a new order

explanation.surface: Gatherings at a country house are organised in a Gloucestershire town.
explanation.walkthrough: Stroud is a town in Gloucestershire. 'House parties' is the members of a royal house, here the dynasty of Henry VIII.
explanation.definitionFit: The members of the English royal dynasty from 1485 to 1603 are its parties.

clue.text: Medicinal extract in the heater is about £1

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: about says the sun word goes around the pound letters

parts.note: the sun is what heats the earth
L stands for a pound and I is Roman one

explanation.surface: A medicine inside a heater apparently costs a pound.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'in' is taken literally, not as a container signal; £1 supplies L for pound plus Roman I.
explanation.definitionFit: Insulin is a hormone extracted, originally from animal pancreas, for treating diabetes.

clue.text: Outbids many in working dress

indicators.note: in says the letter for many sits inside the clothing word

parts.note: overalls are protective clothing for work
C, Roman 100, stands for many

explanation.surface: Many workers in overalls are making higher offers.
explanation.walkthrough: In bridge, to overcall is to bid over an opponent's bid.
explanation.definitionFit: To overcall in bridge is to make a higher bid than the previous player.

clue.text: Punitive taxes ?

parts.note: taxes laid on people, and also school punishments of extra lines or work

explanation.surface: Heavy levies meant to punish.
explanation.walkthrough: Impositions are both levies and, in British schools, extra written tasks given as punishment ('impots').
explanation.definitionFit: Levies imposed on people are impositions, and the word also names punishment tasks set at school.

clue.text: A bit of a certainty of course, the favourite

parts.note: on the racecourse a snip is a horse thought certain to win
a favourite is a pet

explanation.surface: A racing tipster offers a sure thing: back the favourite.
explanation.walkthrough: SNIP is British racing slang for a near-certain winner or a bargain; 'of course' points to the racecourse.
explanation.definitionFit: A snippet is a small piece or fragment of something.

clue.text: One is not always entitled to be so addressed

definitions.text: One is not always entitled to be so addressed

parts.words: One is not always entitled to be so addressed
parts.note: a polite form of address that is also a knight's title, so not everyone called it holds the title

explanation.surface: A remark on whether one deserves a particular form of address.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Entitled' means holding a title: a knight has the title, but any man may be addressed this way politely.
explanation.definitionFit: A knight bears this title, yet schoolboys use it for any teacher, without entitlement.

clue.text: Risks being tempted into mischief, perhaps

definitions.text: Risks being tempted into mischief, perhaps

parts.words: Risks being tempted into mischief, perhaps
parts.note: recalls the saying that the devil finds work for unoccupied hands

explanation.surface: Someone at risk of temptation.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'the devil makes work for idle hands': one who does nothing is open to mischief.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who does nothing, lazing about, invites the devil's mischief, per the proverb.

clue.text: Saw one in the O.T.?

explanation.surface: A woodworking tool spotted in the Old Testament.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saw' is a noun meaning a saying, not the tool; Proverbs is a book of the Old Testament.
explanation.definitionFit: A saw is an old saying, and the Book of Proverbs is in the Old Testament.

clue.text: The tanks repaired in USSR

indicators.note: repaired says the letters are rebuilt into a new order

explanation.surface: Tanks are fixed up in the Soviet Union.
explanation.walkthrough: Tashkent, capital of Uzbekistan, was a Soviet city when this was set.
explanation.definitionFit: Tashkent was a major city of the Soviet Union, capital of the Uzbek SSR.

clue.text: Barker's complaint might change the colour scheme

explanation.surface: A complaint from a dog, and a decorating job.
explanation.walkthrough: The barker is a dog; distemper is also a cheap water-based paint for walls.
explanation.definitionFit: Distemper is a viral disease of dogs, and also a kind of wall paint that would alter a room's colours.

clue.text: Pride of the side ?

parts.note: a pride is a group of big cats, and the British rugby touring side carries the same big-cat name

explanation.surface: Praise for a team's star.
explanation.walkthrough: A pride is the collective noun for these big cats, and the British and Irish touring rugby team is named after them.
explanation.definitionFit: A pride is the group noun for these maned cats, and the rugby side is called after them.

clue.text: About 100, to include one souvenir

parts.note: re means about or concerning

indicators.note: to include tells us the pair of letters holds the word for one

parts.note: L is the pound sign's letter and C is Roman 100
one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: Paying around a hundred pounds for a keepsake.
explanation.walkthrough: The OCR dropped the £ sign; the page has '£100', giving L (librum, pound) and C (100), with I placed between them.
explanation.definitionFit: A relic is an object kept as a memento of the past, a keepsake.

clue.text: Spanish explorer's summit, as it were ?

parts.note: Hernando de Soto was a Spanish explorer of North America; with the possessive he gives his name plus S
a summit is a peak

explanation.surface: A mountain top named after a Spanish explorer.
explanation.walkthrough: The mountain belonging to de Soto would be Soto's Peak; run together it is the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a hedge meaning in a manner of speaking, used just like 'as it were'.

clue.text: Criminals like the Vicar of Bray ?

definitions.text: Criminals like the Vicar of Bray ?

parts.words: Criminals like the Vicar of Bray
parts.note: convicts serve sentences, while the vicar of the song changed his beliefs to suit each reign

explanation.surface: Comparing a famous clergyman to lawbreakers.
explanation.walkthrough: The Vicar of Bray, in an old English song, switched religion with every monarch to keep his living; criminals serve time in jail.
explanation.definitionFit: Opportunists who adapt to whoever is in power are trimmers, and convicts doing their sentence also fit.

clue.text: Abolition for novel? Just the reverse

definitions.text: Abolition for novel? Just the reverse

parts.words: Abolition for novel? Just the reverse
parts.note: rather than abolition being swapped for a novel, a novel was written to promote abolition of slavery

explanation.surface: A puzzled note about exchanging abolition for a book.
explanation.walkthrough: Harriet Beecher Stowe's 1852 novel was a famous spur to the anti-slavery cause: a novel for abolition, the reverse of the clue's words.
explanation.definitionFit: Stowe's antislavery novel did much to rally support for ending slavery in America.

clue.text: Bird seen on a river is the American titmouse

parts.note: a chick is a young bird
the Dee is a river in Britain

explanation.surface: A small bird by a river turns out to be an American species.
explanation.walkthrough: The Dee is a river in Wales, England and Scotland; 'seen on' and 'is' only link.
explanation.definitionFit: The black-capped tit of North America is named for its call.

clue.text: Does for the main drainage system ?

explanation.surface: Something that deals with the main drains.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Does for' means ruins; 'the main' is the sea, and a ship's deck drains through holes in its sides.
explanation.definitionFit: To scupper a plan is to wreck it, and a ship's deck openings that let seawater out bear the same name.

clue.text: Many a girl aware of being snobbish, perhaps

parts.note: a school class holds many girls
conscious means aware

explanation.surface: A girl who knows how she is perceived turns out to be a snob.
explanation.walkthrough: A school class is a group of many pupils, here girls.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone preoccupied with social rank may be snobbish, which is why 'perhaps' qualifies it.

clue.text: Took up poet dad found confusing

indicators.note: confusing says the letters of these words are muddled into a new order

explanation.surface: A poet finds his father bewildering.
explanation.walkthrough: 'found' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: To take up a cause or a child is to embrace it as one's own.

clue.text: Unavailing demand for economy

explanation.surface: A fruitless call for thrift.
explanation.walkthrough: Split it in two and it becomes an order to consume less.
explanation.definitionFit: Something futile is of no help, and split in two words the answer is an instruction to consume less.

clue.text: College puts up our Mr French

indicators.note: puts up, in a down clue, says the letters run from the bottom upward

parts.note: notre is French for our
M is the abbreviation of Monsieur, French for Mr

explanation.surface: A college gives a Frenchman lodging.
explanation.walkthrough: 'French' governs both words: NOTRE and M read upwards make the name.
explanation.definitionFit: Merton is one of the colleges of Oxford University.

clue.text: Charlotte's teacher at Holmes's breakfast-table

explanation.surface: A tutor of Charlotte's sits at the famous detective's breakfast table.
explanation.walkthrough: Charlotte Bronte wrote the novel The Professor about a teacher; Oliver Wendell Holmes wrote The Professor at the Breakfast-Table. The Holmes is not Sherlock.
explanation.definitionFit: Bronte's novel's title character is a teacher, and Oliver Wendell Holmes's essay series has an academic at breakfast.

clue.text: Weird lake, say ?

indicators.note: say marks a word that sounds like the name of the lake

parts.note: Lake Erie is one of the Great Lakes

explanation.surface: Something strange about a lake.
explanation.definitionFit: Something uncanny or strange is weird.

clue.text: University retreat in East Staffordshire town

indicators.note: to retreat is to go backwards, so the town's name is read in reverse

parts.note: Leek is a market town in Staffordshire

explanation.surface: A university's quiet retreat in an English county town.
explanation.walkthrough: Leek is a market town in north Staffordshire, England; 'retreat' turns it to KEEL. The word 'in' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: Keele University is a campus university in Staffordshire, England.

clue.text: Go into some recent errors?

indicators.note: some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Someone is asked to look into a few recent mistakes.
explanation.definitionFit: To go into a room is to come inside it.

clue.text: Correction — make repair in the morning, before ten anyhow

indicators.note: in says the repair word sits inside the morning letters

parts.note: AM stands for ante meridiem, the morning
to mend is to make a repair

indicators.note: anyhow says the letters of ten are arranged in no particular order

explanation.surface: A note to fix something early, before ten o'clock at any rate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'anyhow' gives ENT from ten; 'before' simply places the morning container ahead of it.
explanation.definitionFit: An amendment is a change made to correct or improve a text.

clue.text: A vessel that bore Balaam

parts.note: SS stands for steamship

explanation.surface: A ship that carried a biblical prophet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vessel' suggests a ship but supplies only SS; in Numbers 22 Balaam rode a donkey that spoke to him.
explanation.definitionFit: Balaam's donkey carried him in the Book of Numbers.

clue.text: A feeling of — and longing" (Longfellow)

parts.note: fill the gap in the line from Longfellow's poem The Day Is Done

explanation.surface: A quotation with a missing word.
explanation.walkthrough: Longfellow's The Day Is Done has the line 'A feeling of sadness and longing'.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word names sorrow, a feeling the poem pairs with longing.

clue.text: Felt worn out on the ranch?

definitions.text: Felt worn out on the ranch?

parts.words: Felt worn out on the ranch?
parts.note: read felt as a fabric, a hat made of felt worn outdoors by a cowboy

explanation.surface: A rancher feeling exhausted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Felt' seems to be the verb with 'worn out' meaning tired; it is the cloth, worn out of doors on a ranch.
explanation.definitionFit: This broad-brimmed felt hat is the classic cowboy headgear.
